author: Pedini
text:
Heya Cas,

When drawing Compression PAZ's which is what I drew up on my gold chart,
 you want to be absolutely sure that price is going to go to the other
end of the compression. The only way to do this is to make sure the last
 pocket of supply or demand has been engulfed. Until this happens, we
don't know compression is going to work and really it can go on forever
(just look at AUDNZD).

Looking at your lines now:

1 - This was a test of a flip level, it formed the drop base rally at 4,
 but there is still supply above us (so its not the edge of our PAZ)

2 - Again even if this level is broken, which it was, there still remains to be supply above that needs to break.

Finally price breaks into our PAZ at 3. This was the last of the supply
till the other side of the zone and that is why it is our PAZ level. You
 can see price then retraced tested out Drop Base Rally at 4 and
continued through the zone.

I hope this helps,

Peds

author: Pedini
text:
Hey Cas,

Essentially every bar on the charts is part of one PAZ or another. There
 are all different types. A consolidation in price is a PAZ in itself,
it is when this price zone breaks that we get an idea the direction it
is going to go, and we can use other price action concepts to enter into
 a trade. Hopefully this will get a little clearer in the coming weeks.

author: Spongiform
text:
Hiya Pedini,

Please excuse me while I jump onto your journal!

I've seen it written elsewhere on RTM that 'FTR = FL', but you seem to
treat it differently, and in a way that chimes with how I've come to
think of it.

So, it seems to me that the FTR is just confirmation that the FL is
current, willing Supply / Demand, but this does not mean that the FTR is
 current, willing Supply / Demand in and of itself (whether it is or
isn't depends on the structure and location of the FTR to my mind).

It's this FTR confirmation of the FL which enables us to determine where
 PAZes are bounded, and where to look for EGs, which show us that
current, willing Supply / Demand has now been absorbed, so price will
only find more at the next confirmed level out (explaining why price
will likely move from one edge of a PAZ to another edge of the adjoining
 PAZ)... .

My conclusion is actually that 'FTR (usually) = FTB' - and thus the FL
has already been tested and Supply / Demand removed from it. Perhaps the
 subtle difference is a matter of how quickly the FL is tested after it
is formed?

Am I on the right track or wide of the mark?

Thanks in advance.

Spongy.

author: Pedini
text:
Hey guy, just got back from a weekend away, I read your comment on the
 weekend, but wasn't ready to put my mind from "Break mode" to "Chart
mode". Anyway, back into it, YIPEE!

Spongy - Going from your comment, and some of your articles you have put
 together, you really have a talent for tieing information together! As
for your question, in my mind this is how I see it (and it may be a
simplistic way of viewing it). A FTR is when a level is broken and price
 fails to get back to higher/lower prices, this failure can be a test of
 the broken level, or it may fall short, but it is still a FTR.

Now, as for your comment regarding a FTR testing and thus removing
supply/demand from a flag, again you have this correct IMO, but you may
be missing something. I remember when I first started on supply/demand
trading I used to watch Sam Seidens webinars. Now Mr Seiden is very
strict on teaching not trading a level that is a test of another level
(which in our case can be a FTR). To me this is nonsense, just think
about how compression forms for example, every time supply/demand is
tested in compression it is testing a test of another level, so these
levels work!

You also have the idea behind the PAZ down well. For me the FTR is more
important to engulf and then to look for a trade, rather than basing a
trade on the FTR itself (unless it was preceded by an engulf of another
FTR). This is all a little bit of a mouthful, I hope it's understood!

Hoto - I didn't mark out any CP because there was nothing important to
mark off, and as you see the trade was not based on cany CP. You are
spot on, those are the exact reasons I marked off those FTR levels

Peds

author: Spongiform
text:
Hiya Pedini,

Hope you had a nice break, if you're based in the UK, we had (are having) some pretty nice weather at long last!

Thanks for your reply, I attended Sam Seiden's webinars as well: I still
 have that 'retest of level' bias, it's going slowly, but I don't think
I'll ever be comfortable as a 'range' trader... .

I agree with your comment that the FTR doesn't have to be at the same
level as the FL, to me it just confirms what the FL represents.
Referring back to my bias - my current way of thinking is that if the
FTR is at the same level, the FL is the source, but if the FTR is lower
or higher, then the FTR is the new source (preferably lower if the
general direction is down and higher if it's up, but rightly or wrongly
I'm agnostic at this time). In the same vein, Compression is
progressively higher FTRs, so I can be okay with that too, but I need to
 get a sense of direction to take advantage of these, something I lack
in the chart world (quite the opposite to my sense of direction in the
real world)!

It's that inability to determine direction that's holding me back, but
the EG of a confirmed level might be my guiding star if I can nail the
combo. I'll get there eventually - just have to keep on keeping on until
 I do.

Regards.

Spongy.
